opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the deep reason is that Go is, to a very good approximation, a Markovian game. If you hand me a board position and tell me whose turn it is, everything you need to know to play optimally from that point forward is basically right there on the board. How you got to that position doesn't change the value of the position or what the best move is. That's a really nice property, and it's not true of most of the world.

I'd add one small caveat to the framing, which is that the AlphaGo family didn't throw away history *entirely*. In the later versions, like AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero, the input actually stacks the last several board positions. Part of that is a technicality: rules like ko and superko forbid repeating positions, so you need a bit of history to know which moves are legal. And part of it, I think, is that the history acts as a kind of attention signal. It tells the network where the action has been, which is useful even if it isn't strictly necessary.

But the philosophy is still right. They're not trying to model the opponent's psychology or replay the narrative of the game. They're saying: here's the state, what's the value, what's the policy. And that's what makes the whole self-play plus tree search machine work so cleanly. MCTS assumes you can plug in a state, roll forward, and evaluate. If the true state depended on some long hidden history, that whole approach gets much messier.

What I find interesting is the contrast with what we're doing now in robotics and language models. In the real world you almost never have a clean Markov state. A robot's camera image right now doesn't tell you if the drawer was opened a minute ago, or what the person asked you to do. So you're forced to carry history, whether that's a long context window or some learned memory. In a sense, a lot of modern AI is about *constructing* a Markov state out of a messy history. Go gave it to you for free, and that's a big part of why it was such a tractable domain to crack first.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss 2v2 Go or using play history to infer a partner’s strategy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that Go is basically a Markov game. The board tells you everything you need to know about the future. It doesn't matter how the stones got there, the set of legal moves and the eventual outcome depend only on what's on the board right now. There are tiny exceptions, like ko rules where you can't repeat a prior position, and that's actually why AlphaGo fed in a few previous frames rather than literally a single snapshot. But for all practical purposes the history is redundant.

And when you have a Markovian state, carrying history around is not just unnecessary, it's actively harmful. You're giving the network more inputs to overfit to. The policy could start keying off of, "oh, my opponent played this opening sequence, so they're probably this kind of player," and that's a spurious signal when you're training against yourself through self-play anyway. Dropping the history is a strong inductive bias that says: the position is what matters, learn to evaluate positions.

What I find interesting is how much that choice doesn't transfer to the problems I care about, which is robotics. In the real world, you almost never have the full state. The camera doesn't tell you how heavy the cup is, whether the drawer is stuck, what's behind the object you're reaching for. All of that has to be inferred from how the interaction has gone so far, which means history is doing real work. It's carrying your belief about the hidden variables. So in robot learning you end up wanting the opposite design, something like a recurrent or transformer policy that attends over the last several seconds of observations and actions.

There's a subtler reason history matters for robots too, which is that you're often learning from human demonstrations. Humans are not Markov policies. They have intentions that span many timesteps, and if you train a one-frame behavior cloning policy on that data, the same image gets mapped to several different actions depending on what the person was in the middle of doing. The policy averages them and you get this mushy, hesitant behavior. Giving the model context lets it disambiguate which plan it's executing.

So I'd say AlphaGo got it exactly right for Go, and the lesson isn't "don't use history," it's "match your state representation to how much of the world is actually observable." Go is the rare case where it all is.

r001.rationale: The response says Go is effectively Markovian and that the board state is sufficient, but it does not state that Go admits a Nash equilibrium strategy depending only on the current board.

r002.rationale: It mentions conditioning on an opponent’s opening sequence as a potentially spurious signal, but does not say that exploiting a known opponent bias can outperform a Nash equilibrium strategy.

r003.rationale: The response discusses history in robotics, but does not mention 2v2 Go or inferring a partner’s playing strategy from game history.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as choosing a sufficient statistic for the decision you’re trying to make. In Go, the current board tells you almost everything you need to know about what to do next. There are some technical exceptions around repetition rules, but generally you don’t need to know how the stones got there to evaluate the position.

That’s a really useful inductive bias. If two different sequences of moves lead to the same position, you want to reuse what you’ve learned about that position, rather than treat them as different situations. You’re telling the model, “The path you took here is mostly irrelevant. Focus on what’s on the board.”

The interesting question is whether you can do something analogous in less structured environments. In the real world, what you see right now usually isn’t a sufficient statistic. You need memory to infer things that aren’t directly observable. So the challenge becomes learning a representation of the history that preserves what matters for your next decision.

r003.rationale: It mentions memory in less structured environments, but not 2v2 Go or inferring a partner’s strategy from play history.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that the board is essentially a sufficient statistic for deciding what to do next. You don’t need to know the story of how the stones got there; you need to know what moves are available and what their consequences are. There are some technical caveats around repetition rules, but that’s the basic idea.

That’s a very useful property for a learning system. If two different sequences of moves lead to the same position, you can treat them as the same problem instead of learning separate answers for each history. In a lot of real-world tasks, you don’t get that luxury: your current observation doesn’t tell you everything you need to know, so remembering the past becomes part of figuring out the state.
